visual.general_description: General hypokalemia algorithm with three explanatory notes.
visual.detailed_description: On the left, black outlined boxes and thin pale-blue arrows proceed from History and physical exam to questions about GI loss, diuretics, other medications and acute intracellular shift. The Yes branch goes left to a blue Stop box; No goes down-right to Hypertension. Hypertension Yes branches left to Check plasma aldosterone : renin and then “Mineralocorticod excess?” (printed spelling); No branches right to Check urine Na+, K+, Cl−, Cr. This branches downward to three boxes printed “Sureptittuous vomiting/laxative/ diuretic use?”, “Tubolopathy? (eg: Gitelman, Bartter, RTA)” and “Severe hypomegnesia?” (literal printed spellings). On the right, numbered notes discuss disproportionate diuretic hypokalemia, correcting potassium before aldosterone testing/medication context, and urinary-ratio patterns for vomiting/laxatives/diuretics/tubulopathy. Printed thresholds are Na/Cl >1.6 for vomiting, Na/Cl <0.7 for laxatives, and urine K/creatinine >2.5 mmol/mmol for tubulopathy. The subsequent urine Na/Cl expression resembles w1 and is not confidently resolved. No case-specific marker, patient photo or panel letters are present.

evidence.quote: Etiologies of hypokalemia are typically categorized into (1) decreased intake, (2) intracellular shift, and (3) increased loss (renal or extrarenal). Various diagnostic approaches have been proposed to evaluate hypokalemia. Among them, the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) algorithm offers a practical, structured framework for identifying the underlying cause (Figure 3) []. Applying this approach allowed for the identification of distal RTA (type 1 RTA) as the cause of hypokalemia in our patient.
